claims.text: On 12 July 1955 Israel signed a general "Atoms for Peace" agreement with the United States, the second country to do so; in 1955 Ben-Gurion also launched a secret feasibility initiative and delegated it to Shimon Peres.
In July–September 1956 Ernst David Bergmann asked the United States for a reactor and heavy water; the Atomic Energy Commission agreed only under stricter safeguards, and Israel dropped the probe.

On 20 March 1957 Israel signed a contract with the American firm AMF for a 1-megawatt pool reactor at Nahal Soreq; construction began in January 1958, the final contract was signed on 19 March 1958, and the reactor reached criticality in a public ceremony in June 1960.

Bertrand Goldschmidt of France's atomic energy commission (CEA) recalled attending the September 1956 meeting at which Peres asked for French help; the request had two parts, a reactor, which was "relatively easy to agree upon", and a plutonium extraction (reprocessing) plant, which was "quite difficult". Cohen notes that Goldschmidt often said he did not remember.

According to Goldschmidt, the high commissioner Francis Perrin hesitated for weeks over the reprocessing plant until Pierre Guillaumat urged Goldschmidt to persuade him; Perrin later accused Goldschmidt of "extorting" his signature.

The Federation of American Scientists and the Jewish Virtual Library both state that France agreed in autumn 1956 to supply an 18-megawatt (thermal) research reactor, and that a revised agreement signed on 3 October 1957 provided for a 24-megawatt reactor whose cooling and waste systems were designed for three times that power, with a chemical reprocessing plant covered in unwritten protocols.

The National Interest describes the 1957 package as three confidential contracts covering a 24-megawatt heavy-water reactor, a loan of 385 tonnes of natural uranium, joint nuclear-weapons research and production, and backing for a plutonium extraction plant.

The date of signature is reported differently: the Burr–Cohen briefing book gives 3 October 1957 or 30 October 1957; the Center for Israel Education says Prime Minister Maurice Bourgès-Maunoury dated his approval 30 September but signed on 1 October, the day his government fell; Goldschmidt said it was backdated by one day because Bourgès-Maunoury lost a no-confidence vote, and that his successor Félix Gaillard was "totally unaware" of it on taking office.

In his memoir Peres recalled watching Bourgès-Maunoury, after his government had fallen, sign the letter authorizing the reactor sale and date it the previous day: "I asked no questions"; he called it "the most generous display of friendship I had ever known."

The reactor was built in secret at Dimona, outside IAEA inspection, under Colonel Manes Pratt; at the peak about 1,500 Israelis and some French workers were employed; French customs were told the largest components, such as the reactor tank, belonged to a desalination plant bound for Latin America.

Israel and Norway signed a heavy-water agreement on 25 February 1959 under which Norway, through the seller NORATOM, sold Israel 20 tons, shipped via the United Kingdom; the US political officer in Oslo, Richard Kerry, warned that disclosure could embarrass Norway. FAS separately reports that the French Air Force secretly flew up to four tons of heavy water to Israel.

In May 1960 France pressed Israel to disclose the project and accept international inspection, threatening to withhold reactor fuel; de Gaulle offered to sell Israel fighter aircraft in exchange for halting work on the reprocessing plant. The Jewish Virtual Library adds that de Gaulle feared a scandal while France's position was already strained by the Algerian war.

Shlomo Aronson writes that de Gaulle "secretly advised Israel that he had decided to abrogate the 1957 accord", at the moment Pinhas Lavon was reviving the Lavon affair in May 1960, and that this crisis was concealed and became widely known only years later.

Under the compromise reached in 1960, France would supply the uranium and components already ordered and would not insist on inspections, while Israel would state that it had no intention of making atomic weapons, would not reprocess plutonium, would reveal the reactor and would finish it without French help; the Jewish Virtual Library says little changed in practice. The Nuclear Weapon Archive (1997) dates the agreement to November 1960.
According to Aronson, the only public voice of internal controversy over Dimona was the Public Committee for Nuclear Disarmament in the Middle East, led by Yeshayahu Leibowitz and Eliezer Livne.

The Nuclear Weapon Archive calls the Suez Crisis "the genesis of Israel's nuclear weapons production program" and dates a secret meeting of Golda Meir, Peres and the French ministers Pineau and Bourgès-Maunoury to 7 November 1956; it dates groundbreaking at Dimona to early 1958, while the 1961 US scientists were told ground was broken in 1959.

disputes.question: When was the 1957 French–Israeli agreement signed?

positions.view: 3 October 1957 (FAS; Jewish Virtual Library), or 3 or 30 October (Burr and Cohen).
Signed on 1 October and backdated to 30 September, the day before the Bourgès-Maunoury government fell (Center for Israel Education; Goldschmidt's one-day backdating; Peres's memoir).

disputes.question: What did the 1960 Franco-Israeli compromise change?

positions.view: Israel pledged no weapons and no reprocessing and revealed the reactor; work on the plutonium plant halted (FAS; Nuclear Weapon Archive).
Little changed in practice (Jewish Virtual Library); Cohen and Burr later document a concealed underground separation plant (see the Kennedy-era entries).

entries.topic: How the United States found Dimona, April 1958–November 1960

claims.text: On 7 March 1958 State Department Instruction A-128 asked the Tel Aviv embassy for information on Israel's atomic energy program; on 15 April 1958 Second Secretary Lewis Townsend met Bergmann, who called a claim about uranium by one Benard untrue (Tel Aviv Despatch 652, 16 April 1958).

The intelligence post-mortem delivered to Kennedy's office on 31 January 1961 found that information on the site was available to some parts of the intelligence community as early as April 1958 and that site information reaching intelligence channels in mid-1959 "was discounted"; it blamed lost reports and dots "not properly connected", including Bergmann's April 1958 "experimental reactor" remark, which analysts wrongly tied to Soreq.

Whether U-2 photography identified Dimona early is disputed: FAS and the Jewish Virtual Library say U-2 overflights captured its construction in 1958 but the site was not identified as nuclear until 1960; the Nuclear Weapon Archive says US intelligence identified a probable reactor complex before the end of 1958; Burr and Cohen say it is unclear whether U-2 photographs were especially telling and that the photographs of late 1960 came from military attachés.

Burr and Cohen write that the United States first learned of Dimona in mid-summer 1960 from an American corporate official in Tel Aviv: in late July 1960 an AMF employee, D. Anderson, reported after talking to Daniel Kimhi of Naptha Petroleum that French personnel were building "a 60 megawatt atomic power reactor" near Beersheba; Tel Aviv Despatch 75 of 2 August 1960 is the earliest declassified US reference to Dimona.

During a helicopter ride, the Israeli Finance Ministry official Addy Cohen called the site a "textile plant"; the briefing book dates this both to September 1960 and, in one document, to February 1960.

On 22 November 1960 a French CEA official told the AEC's John Rouleau that France was not collaborating with Israel on a power reactor; on 25 November Secretary of State Herter told the British ambassador, Harold Caccia, of a possible plutonium-producing reactor built with French aid.

Henry Gomberg, a University of Michigan nuclear engineering professor, visited Israel and, debriefed in Washington on 1 December 1960, judged the Beersheba site a "large classified project" with a reactor "far beyond any kind of a training reactor" that would be "capable of producing weapons grade plutonium"; he estimated about 250 megawatts thermal and noted its resemblance to France's G-1 reactor at Marcoule.

A Joint Atomic Energy Intelligence Committee report of 2 December 1960, "Israeli Plutonium Production", referred to a "plutonium separation plant"; the National Security Archive's 2024 release calls it the first and only known US intelligence report to state that Dimona would include a reprocessing plant, a question later US intelligence treated as unsettled until the late 1960s.

Special National Intelligence Estimate 100-8-60 of 8 December 1960 judged that "plutonium production for weapons is at least one major purpose" and that Israel "will produce some weapons grade plutonium in 1963-64 and possibly as early as 1962"; the same day CIA Director Allen Dulles briefed the 470th NSC meeting with photographs taken by the US Army attaché, and Herter put the cost at $40–80 million.

Burr and Cohen call the delay "a major blunder, what is called in our times an intelligence failure", comparable to the failures before India's 1974 and 1998 tests, and "a tremendous counterintelligence success for Israel"; they argue that earlier US pressure on France and Norway might have stopped the project.

disputes.question: Did the United States know about Dimona before 1960?

positions.view: Yes in part: U-2 photographs caught construction in 1958 (FAS, JVL), and the Nuclear Weapon Archive says a probable reactor complex was identified before the end of 1958.
Information existed from April 1958 but was discounted or misfiled, so the government did not know until mid-1960 (the 1961 post-mortem as presented by Burr and Cohen).

claims.text: On 7 December 1960 the State Department summoned the Israeli ambassador for an explanation, and at an Operations Coordinating Board luncheon Livingston Merchant said the Department would be "the sole spokesman"; on 9 December Herter showed Ambassador Avraham Harman photographs of the site and called the French chargé d'affaires.

At the NATO meeting in Paris on 16 December 1960 French Foreign Minister Maurice Couve de Murville acknowledged a "replica of [the] Marcoule plant", said France would supply raw materials and receive the plutonium, and, asked about financing, said he "assumed the money came from US."
On 18 December 1960, on NBC's Meet the Press, AEC chairman John McCone said Israel had not "revealed" the reactor to the United States.

At a meeting with his advisers on 19 December 1960 Eisenhower said "we do not know where they have obtained the funds", that the United States had an interest in knowing "because of the aid we are giving them", and cited evidence of a cost of $100–200 million; Defense Secretary Thomas Gates said "our information is that the plant is not for peaceful uses" and McCone said "there is a chemical separation plant there"; Eisenhower agreed Israel should allow IAEA-type inspection. Allen Dulles said Israel was trying to confuse Dimona, "a large production installation", with the small Soreq reactor.

On 20 December 1960 Harman told Herter that Israel was "building an additional research reactor of 24 megawatts capacity in the Negev", that "a reactor of this size is not of industrial importance", that it had been begun a year earlier and would take three to four years, and that he could not answer what would be done with the plutonium; he cited a French Foreign Office announcement of 19 December giving assurances of peaceful use.

Ben-Gurion told the Knesset the reactor was "exclusively for peaceful purposes" (Burr and Cohen, 2015) and was "a research reactor ... which will serve the needs of industry, agriculture, health, and science" (Cohen and Burr, 2025). The date is given as 21 December 1960 (Nuclear Weapon Archive; one passage of the 2015 briefing book) and as 22 December 1960 (Cohen and Burr, 2025; another passage of the 2015 briefing book).
Addy Cohen told US diplomats on 21–22 December 1960 that Israel had "been misbehaving a little" and that the reactor could be used "for weapons purposes" (Tel Aviv Telegram 574, 23 December).

Meeting Ambassador Ogden Reid on 24 December 1960, Ben-Gurion asked "Why in [the] States is everything being told [to] everybody?"; Cohen and Burr also quote him telling Reid in this period, "we are not a satellite of America ... and will never be a satellite."

A State Department telegram to Tel Aviv at the end of December 1960 said "Neither Dept nor other interested Washington agencies consider Ben Gurion's statements thus far satisfactory", that "USG policy is unequivocally opposed to proliferation of nuclear weapons capabilities", and that Washington would "not welcome new round of alarmist publicity"; another of 31 December cited a "clearly apparent lack of candor", and Merchant recorded Dulles's complaint that Israel had "by no means come clean with us."

On 28 December 1960 the embassy estimated Dimona's cost at $17.8 million in foreign exchange and 29.2 million Israeli pounds, and Reid suggested bringing in the IAEA or internationally known scientists.

On 4 January 1961 Ben-Gurion said Israel "has no plans for producing nuclear weapons" and would not accept IAEA inspection "until all reactors are treated as equals"; the summary the outgoing administration sent to Congress's Joint Committee on Atomic Energy on 19 January 1961 recorded Israel's statement that all plutonium from Dimona "will be returned to France."

Burr and Cohen write that Eisenhower's administration, with weeks left in office, kept the matter under State Department control until Kennedy took office, and that Kennedy then "chose the toughest path of struggle and confrontation" while Johnson "planted the seeds of compromise."

FAS and the Jewish Virtual Library summarize the December 1960 statement as Ben-Gurion describing the Dimona complex as a nuclear research center built for "peaceful purposes"; FAS dates a CIA report on Dimona's implications for proliferation to 8 December 1960.

disputes.question: On what date did Ben-Gurion make his Knesset statement on the reactor?

positions.view: 21 December 1960 (Nuclear Weapon Archive; one passage of the 2015 briefing book).
22 December 1960 (Cohen and Burr, 2025; another passage of the 2015 briefing book). An Israeli MK in 2000 dated it 20 December (not fetched as primary; not used).
Israel's account: a 24-megawatt research reactor for peaceful purposes, plutonium to be returned to France (Harman; Ben-Gurion; the January 1961 summary).
US officials at the time doubted it (Gates, McCone, Dulles; 'lack of candor'), and Cohen and Burr later called the account false, citing the concealed separation plant.

entries.topic: Kennedy's first months and the first American visit to Dimona, January–May 1961

claims.text: In a memorandum of 30 January 1961 Secretary of State Dean Rusk told Kennedy that Ben-Gurion had given "categoric assurances supported by appropriate public statements" that "Israel does not have plans for developing nuclear weaponry", that the Israeli and French assurances "appear to be satisfactory", and that the Department considered this "not a single episode but a continuing subject" requiring "a continuing watch".

Rusk's memorandum said the United States was encouraging Israel to permit "a qualified scientist from the United States or other friendly power to visit the Dimona installation", and recalled that in 1955 under Atoms for Peace the United States had undertaken to help Israel's atomic energy program.

On 31 January 1961 Kennedy met the former ambassador Ogden Reid, who said an inspection could be arranged "if it is done on a secret basis" and that "we can accept at face value Ben Gurion's assurances that the reactor is to be devoted to peaceful purposes."

On 28 March 1961 Assistant Secretary G. Lewis Jones told Harman the United States had been "faithfully waiting since early January" for the promised invitation; Harman suggested no action before Passover.

In April 1961 Harman conveyed "an invitation for an American to visit the Dimona reactor site during the week of May 15", asked that the visit be secret because publicity "could have a most undesirable effect", and called it the discharge of Ben-Gurion's specific promise; Philip Farley warned that labelling it secret "might be counter-productive" and Jones noted "a good deal of Congressional interest".

The National Security Archive records that on 12 April 1961 Harman proposed a Kennedy–Ben-Gurion meeting with the Dimona visit as its tacit condition, and that on 16 May the Israeli diplomat Mordechai Gazit hinted to Farley that Israel might be interested in a nuclear option for deterrence, which the editors read as a possible "trial balloon".

The two AEC scientists were Ulysses M. Staebler and Jesse W. Croach. The dates differ by source: the FRUS editors say the visit accepted on 28 April for 15 May was moved to 18 May; the National Security Archive says they arrived on 17 May and visited Dimona on 20 May, escorted by Ephraim Katzir and Manes Pratt; the Wilson Center archive summary says they toured Israel's nuclear sites from 17 to 22 May 1961.
Foreign Minister Golda Meir reportedly objected to the visit, being "concerned about the implications of misleading the American scientists."

Briefing the State Department on 25 May, the scientists said they were received "with cordiality" and that "nothing was concealed from them"; the complex occupied a square 750 metres a side; the reactor might cost about $15 million with about $20 million more for supporting plant; Israel said ground was broken in 1959 and the reactor would "not be completed before 1964".

Their conclusions: "There is no present evidence that the Israelis have weapon production in mind"; the reactor would eventually produce small quantities of weapons-suitable plutonium like others of its size; Israel's secrecy was "regrettable, but perhaps understandable"; there was "strong evidence of close French scientific collaboration and support". The report Bundy received on 26 May said the reactor was "of the scope and peaceful character previously described to the United States."

Cohen and Burr (2025) write that Pratt's account to the visitors, that Dimona would give "experience in the construction of a nuclear facility which would prepare (Israel) for nuclear power in the long run", was false, that Dimona personnel spent weeks preparing before US teams arrived, and that Israel concealed the underground separation plant; they attribute the deception finding to a 1967 State Department intelligence memorandum and later reporting.

disputes.question: Did the May 1961 visit see what was there?

positions.view: The scientists reported that 'nothing was concealed' and found 'no present evidence' of weapons intent (FRUS; Battle to Bundy).
Cohen and Burr argue the visits were staged and the separation plant hidden, citing a 1967 INR memorandum and later reporting; Meir reportedly worried about misleading the scientists.

claims.text: Kennedy met Ben-Gurion in the President's suite at the Waldorf-Astoria in New York on 30 May 1961, from 4:45 to 6:15 p.m., with Ambassador Harman, Myer Feldman and Assistant Secretary Phillips Talbot present, on Kennedy's way to the Vienna summit with Khrushchev.

In the official memorandum Kennedy described Dimona as "a large reactor, with plutonium producing capability"; Ben-Gurion said Israel's "main—and for the time being, only—purpose is this", meaning economic development including "the economic desalinization of sea water", and that "in three or four years we might have need for a plant to process plutonium."

Kennedy said two American scientists "had given him a good report of it" and asked whether neutral scientists could also observe it; Ben-Gurion asked "who are really neutrals these days?", Kennedy suggested "the Scandinavians and the Swiss", and Ben-Gurion said he had no objection.

On weapons, Ben-Gurion said of Egypt "in ten or fifteen years the Egyptians presumably could achieve it themselves" and "If they should defeat us they would do to the Jews what Hitler did"; Kennedy said "the UAR would not permit Israel to go ahead in this field without getting into it itself."

On Israel's request for missiles Kennedy said "while the Hawk is a defensive weapon it is also a missile", that "we are reluctant to introduce missiles into the Middle East", and that "we do not want to see Israel at a disadvantage."

On refugees Ben-Gurion said the Arab states "regard the refugees as the best weapon at hand" and "don't care what happens to people"; Kennedy referred to the United States paying 70% of UNRWA's costs.

The National Security Archive's draft of the memorandum differs from the official versions: it includes Ben-Gurion's tacit acknowledgment of a weapons potential and a statement suggesting freedom of action on eventual reprocessing; the Israeli minutes record him saying that "for the time being, the only purposes" were "for peace" and "we will see what happens in the Middle East."

The National Security Archive says Dimona took "no more than ten to fifteen minutes" of a meeting of about an hour and a half, that Kennedy "exerted no new pressure", and quotes a biographer: "Ben Gurion felt relieved. The reactor was saved, at least for the time being"; it judges that the confrontation was postponed for two years.

Briefing the representatives of ten Arab states afterwards, Talbot said Ben-Gurion's assurance that the program was "for peaceful purposes only" was firm and that Kennedy had expressed concern about proliferation and satisfaction with the assurances; the Sudanese ambassador asked about "Israel's second reactor", and Talbot said the Iraqi ambassador's question about US arms aid to Israel was not pursued at the meeting.

At the Arab briefing the Department's public statement on refugees said the United States "will fully support moves made by the Commission" (the Palestine Conciliation Commission), and Ben-Gurion's reported comment on the Commission was "It's worth a try."

A circular telegram of 17 June 1961 reported the inspection's results to US posts; on 26 September 1962 Israeli officials took two visiting AEC scientists to Dimona without warning for a 40-minute tour, after which a State Department circular drafted on 24 October 1962 reported "no evidence of preparation for nuclear weapons production" and "Work on reactor progressing normally."
The October 1962 circular instructed the Cairo embassy, in connection with the Cuban crisis, to renew to Nasser the assurances of June 1961 about Dimona.

Counts of US visits in the 1960s differ: Cohen and Burr give eight between 1961 and 1969, seven of them after Kennedy forced regular visits in 1963; FAS says seven during the 1960s, tightly controlled by Israel.

disputes.question: What did Ben-Gurion tell Kennedy about Dimona's purpose?

positions.view: A peaceful purpose 'for the time being' (official memorandum; Israeli minutes), with a possible plutonium plant in three or four years.
The unedited draft shows a tacit acknowledgment of weapons potential and freedom of action on reprocessing (National Security Archive).

claims.text: Ben-Gurion wrote to his daughter on 15 September 1957 that the Middle East had only two stable states, Turkey and Israel, and on 16 October 1957 recorded in his diary that Israel and Turkey were the only stable, free and democratic countries in the region (as cited by Alon Liel).
Ethiopia's Emperor Haile Selassie initiated contact in February 1957 through Israel's defence ministry delegation in Paris (Schonmann).

On 15 December 1957 Israel's ambassador to Italy, Eliyahu Sasson, met Turkish Prime Minister Adnan Menderes in Paris and proposed linking the Mossad with Turkey's intelligence service; at a follow-up in early April 1958 Menderes proposed a coup in Syria, which Ben-Gurion rejected (Schonmann).

Schonmann writes that the foundations of the policy, which Israeli documents call the "Outer Circle", were in place by the Syrian crisis of August 1957, and that Ben-Gurion presented the plan to his government on 20 July 1958, when it was adopted as state policy; she cites Israel State Archives minutes of the government meetings of 20 and 28 July 1958 and of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Security Committee of 16 July and 19 August 1958.

On 24 July 1958 Ben-Gurion wrote to Eisenhower seeking US support for a pact of Turkey, Iran, Ethiopia and Sudan with Israel, describing it as "a strong dam against the Nasserist–Soviet torrent" (Schonmann's rendering; Liel's German translation reads "a strong dam against Nasser's wild Sovietism"); Eisenhower replied on 25 July promising a fuller answer from Dulles.

Schonmann writes that the plan aimed at "political friendship" with non-Arab states rather than military aid, and at creating "a phantom of a pact" to persuade Washington of Israel's regional value; Mossad chief Isser Harel described Israel as possibly "the long arm" of the United States in Asia and Africa.

A secret, formal political agreement between the Israeli and Turkish prime ministers was signed in August 1958 (Schonmann). Liel and Amotz Asa-El describe a secret visit by Ben-Gurion to Ankara; Asa-El says the two leaders agreed to upgrade relations to full embassies, whereas Liel writes that relations reached ambassadorial level only in January 1992. A Turkish research site citing Israel's published foreign-policy documents lists the agreed points: closer political, military, economic and cultural ties, cooperation between the General Staffs, and the return of envoys to their posts.

After October 1958 the Trident brought the heads of the Israeli, Turkish and Iranian secret services together in semi-annual conferences, with Ethiopia joining later (Schonmann); Yossi Alpher, a former Israeli intelligence officer, dates the first trilateral meeting to late September–early October 1958 and says Israel informed the Americans as soon as it was concluded.

Alpher says the Trident's "primary purpose" was intelligence on Syria, Iraq and Soviet penetration, run by the Mossad directly under the prime minister; that CIA money built a Trident headquarters near Tel Aviv, which the Mossad turned "into a training facility very quickly"; and that Turkish scholars told him "no more than 20 people in Turkey" knew of it.

Alpher says Israel's presence in Tehran was formally a trade delegation and that Turkey, Iran and Ethiopia all "kept it at low level to keep their Arab friends happy"; he summarizes Ben-Gurion's pitch to Washington as "you've got NATO, we have Trident" and says Dulles gave a "lukewarm blessing".

In a telegram reporting Ben-Gurion's account of his secret talk with Iran's General Teymur Bakhtiar, the US embassy recorded that Israeli policy aimed in part to strengthen relations with Turkey, Iran, Ethiopia and Sudan, and possibly later Iraq.

Alpher lists the periphery as one of Ben-Gurion's grand strategies: "periphery doctrine is one, a nuclear deterrent is another, a great power, or super power ally, is a third", the fourth being mass immigration.

Alpher judged the periphery "on balance ... a strategic success" while calling the partners "fair-weather friends, to a large extent"; a review of his book summarizes his finding that the Trident was lopsided, with Iran and Turkey exploiting Israeli intelligence.

disputes.question: How did Washington receive the periphery pact?

positions.view: With a 'lukewarm blessing' from Dulles (Alpher's account).

With caution: the Policy Planning Staff wrote on 11 August 1958 that 'the cornerstone of the suggested entente is not firm', and Dulles approved on 18 August 'extreme caution in giving Ben-Gurion further encouragement or support' (Schonmann, from US archives).

disputes.question: Did the August 1958 Turkish–Israeli agreement raise relations to embassy level?

positions.view: Yes, agreed in principle (Asa-El).
Ambassadorial relations came only in January 1992 (Liel); the agreed text provided for envoys to return to their posts (STRASAM, citing Israeli documents).

Shahrough Akhavi, "Egypt vii. Political and religious relations with Persia in the modern period", Encyclopaedia Iranica VIII/3 (1998)
Paul Iddon, "High points, low points: A history of Iran-Egypt relations", The New Arab (15 February 2019)
"Israel's Periphery Doctrine and Search for Middle East Allies", Brookings Institution event transcript, Yossi Alpher with Bruce Riedel (12 March 2015)

claims.text: Schonmann writes that oil trade between Iran and Israel began quietly in late 1956 at Iran's initiative; that in 1957 SAVAK's director, General Teymur Bakhtiar, met an Israeli representative in Paris and the Shah wanted the Mossad to train Iranian agents in surveillance and listening techniques; that high-level visits and liaison exchanges followed by November 1957; and that Isser Harel visited Tehran in late February 1958.

A US embassy telegram printed in FRUS reports Ben-Gurion's account of a secret talk with Bakhtiar around 27 July, whom he called the "No. 2 man Iran who had ear of Shah": Bakhtiar said Iran felt "let down" by the United States because Turkey and Pakistan received far more arms, and asked whether Iran "should … turn to Russia"; Ben-Gurion replied that Iran had no alternative to close alliance with the West.

The same telegram notes that several Israeli cultural and agricultural experts had visited Iran at Iran's request, that one Israeli was a consultant to Iran's Ministry of Agriculture, and that Israel depended on Iran for the oil for the Eilat pipeline under a contract recently signed with the Rothschild group.

The FRUS editors' note to the telegram records that on 24 July the Shah announced Iran's de facto recognition of Israel, saying it had existed since 1949 although Iran's envoy had been recalled from Tel Aviv in 1951, and that de jure recognition had never been in question; after Arab and especially Nasser's criticism, Iran declared the United Arab Republic's representative in Tehran persona non grata.

Encyclopaedia Iranica dates the press conference to July 1960: asked whether Iran would recognize Israel, the Shah said Iran "had recognized Israel years ago"; Nasser attacked his "pro-Zionist" policies and broke diplomatic relations; the Shah denied any change in Iran's dealings with Israel since 1950.

Iranica records a telegram to the Shah from Shaltut saying the recognition hurt Egyptian sentiment and the feelings of al-Azhar's 'ulama, and suggests the break may have owed more to Iran's growing ties with the Arab Gulf states than to Israel.

The New Arab reports that Nasser denounced the Shah for "selling himself cheaply to imperialism and Zionism", that Foreign Minister Abbas Aram called Nasser a "feeble-minded pharaoh of Egypt", and that in 1958 the Shah secretly arranged with Israel to set up an anti-Nasser broadcasting station at Ahvaz in Khuzestan.
Alpher, a former Israeli intelligence officer, says Israel's presence in Tehran was formally a trade delegation and was kept at a low level so as not to offend Iran's Arab partners.

disputes.question: When did Iran recognize Israel de facto?

positions.view: 1949, according to the Shah's July 1960 statement as summarized by the FRUS editors.
1950 (The New Arab; Iranica's 'since 1950').

disputes.question: Why did Nasser break with Iran in July 1960?

positions.view: Over the Shah's statement on recognizing Israel (FRUS editors; The New Arab).
Possibly more over Iran's ties with the Arab Gulf states (Akhavi, Iranica).

entries.topic: 1958: the United Arab Republic, Lebanon's crisis, the Iraqi revolution and the US and British landings

sources.label: "U.S. Intervention in Lebanon (1958)": compiled US documents (Eisenhower Doctrine message, SNIE 36.4–58 of 5 June 1958, White House memoranda and Eisenhower–Macmillan call of 14 July 1958, message to Congress of 15 July 1958), martinkramer.org
Bruce Riedel, "1958: When America first went to war in the Middle East", Brookings (2 July 2018)
Byron Cannon, "Middle East Turmoil Leads to U.N. Action in Lebanon", EBSCO Research Starters (2021)
Jacob Boswall, "1950s U.S. Foreign Policy Looms Large in Lebanon", New Lines Magazine (29 July 2022)
Alon Liel, "Die strategische Partnerschaft zwischen der Türkei und Israel", Austrian Federal Ministry of Defence publication (c. 2001), pp. 57–64
FRUS 1958–1960, vol. XIII, doc. 31: Memorandum of a Conversation (Dulles, Eban, Shiloah), London, 27 July 1958

claims.text: Egypt and Syria formed the United Arab Republic in February 1958, with Nasser as its ruler; the rival Arab Union of Jordan and Iraq lasted from February to August 1958.

Unrest in Lebanon began in May 1958 when President Camille Chamoun appeared to seek a second term; the US Special National Intelligence Estimate 36.4–58 of 5 June 1958 said "the present conflict was touched off by indications that Christian President Chamoun intended to amend the constitution."

Riedel describes a rebellion by Lebanon's Muslim population and some Christians against a term the article calls unconstitutional; Chamoun blamed Nasser for arms smuggling, but UN inspectors did not support his allegations. New Lines adds that Chamoun's forces killed several Nasserite protesters and that a small civil war followed between pro-Chamoun Christian militias and Nasser-inspired Sunni and Shiite fighters.
In June 1958 the UN Security Council sent the UN Observation Group in Lebanon (UNOGIL), nearly 600 strong, staffing 49 observer posts.

SNIE 36.4–58 judged that Israel "would probably avoid direct involvement", and CIA Director Dulles said "Israel will probably stay out" if the United States intervened; the estimate expected the Soviet reaction to be "confined to vigorous diplomatic and propaganda action" unless US forces fought on UAR territory.

On 14 July 1958 an army coup in Baghdad, which surprised US and British intelligence, killed King Faisal II, the crown prince and the prime minister, Nuri al-Sa'id; Dulles reported that day that "the Crown Prince has been killed, and perhaps Nuri also." Liel writes that the Baghdad Pact thereby lost its main pillar and Turkey sought closer ties with Israel.

Eisenhower convened the NSC on 14 July and, in his memoirs, wrote "we feared the worst…the complete elimination of Western influence in the Middle East"; on 15 July US Marines landed near Beirut (Operation Blue Bat), about 1,700 in the first contingent at Khalde, backed by three carrier groups; Macmillan referred on 14 July to a planned British contingent of "about 3,700", and British paratroopers flew to Amman to support King Hussein.

Peak US strength is given as "almost 15,000" Marines and soldiers (Riedel), about 14,000 (Cannon), and never more than 14,000 (New Lines); one American died from sniper fire (Cannon adds three accidental deaths); the intervention cost about $200 million (New Lines); all US forces had left by 25 October 1958.

General Fuad Chehab, commander of the Lebanese army, was chosen in 1958 as the compromise successor to Chamoun (Cannon dates this to October; New Lines says Nasser favoured the outcome); Riedel writes that the US ambassador disobeyed instructions to broker the army's escort of the Marines, and that Senators John F. Kennedy and J. William Fulbright opposed the intervention, Kennedy arguing that Nasser was not a Soviet puppet.

In London on 27 July 1958 Israel's envoys Abba Eban and Reuven Shiloah told Dulles that Israel had no expansionist ideas and would not seek to take the West Bank if that could be avoided, but wished to avoid hostile forces on its border, and that Ben-Gurion believed Jordan "could be preserved only if anti-Nasser forces in the area cooperated among themselves"; Dulles judged Nasser's anger at the landings reflected their checking his success.
Eisenhower's letter to Ben-Gurion of 25 July 1958 said Israel could "be confident of United States interest in the integrity and independence of Israel".

disputes.question: How many US troops went into Lebanon in 1958?

positions.view: Almost 15,000 at the peak (Riedel).
About 14,000, never more (Cannon; New Lines).
Chamoun's bid for an unconstitutional second term and domestic sectarian politics (SNIE 36.4–58; Riedel; New Lines).
Nasser's subversion and arms smuggling, as Chamoun charged; UN inspectors did not support the charge (Riedel).

entries.topic: The overflight crisis of August 1958: Israel's airspace, the Soviet note and Dulles

sources.label: Noa Schonmann, "Fortitude at stake: the accidental crisis in American–Israeli relations, August 1958", Israel Affairs (2017), doi 10.1080/13537121.2017.1333734
FRUS 1958–1960, vol. XIII, doc. 34: Telegram from the Embassy in Israel (Lawson) to the Department of State, 2 August 1958
FRUS 1958–1960, vol. XIII, doc. 35: Memorandum of a Conversation, Dulles's residence, 3 August 1958, "Israeli Decision to Request U.S. to Cease Overflights of Israel"
FRUS 1958–1960, vol. XIII, doc. 36: Memorandum of a Conversation, Department of State, 5 August 1958, "Use of Israel Airspace for Airlift to Jordan"
The Detroit Jewish News, 8 August 1958, p. 1 (JTA reports)

claims.text: According to a JTA report of 8 August 1958, Israel had first permitted British paratroop overflights to Jordan about three weeks earlier, hoping for firmer Western action against Nasser.

On 1 August 1958 the Soviet Union sent Israel a note calling it "an immediate associate" in aggressive acts against Arab countries; Ben-Gurion's diary called the note "paved with threats to the 'national interests' of Israel". The same day Dulles dated his reply to the periphery letter: "we are prepared to do what we can to be of assistance" and "we believe that Israel should be in a position to deter an attempt at aggression by indigenous forces"; the embassy received it on 2 August and delivered it on 4 August.

On 2 August 1958 Israel's Assistant Director General Comay told the US ambassador, Lawson, that overflights "by US planes must stop immediately", with "no flights even tonight", and Ben-Gurion made the same demand of the British; Lawson judged that Ben-Gurion "does not feel he has firm basis to resist strong Cabinet and potential public opposition to overflights", and Comay called the Soviet note "firm and threatening".

On 3 August, at Dulles's residence, with Ambassador Eban and Minister Yaacov Herzog, Dulles called it "particularly shocking that Israel would do this without any consultation with the US"; he reminded them that "the Eisenhower Doctrine made clear" the United States would support Israel if attacked by a Communist power and asked whether Israel felt "so menaced by the USSR that it would do whatever the Soviet Union requested." Schonmann quotes him calling the step "a show of fear for the Russians to behold".
Eban explained that the British request "involved the sending of additional troops into Jordan", which were "an added convenience but not crucial".

On 5 August Eban, Herzog and Shimon Peres gave Acting Secretary Herter Ben-Gurion's letter consenting to resumed US airlift flights; Eban said Israel's doubts had not stemmed from the Soviet note, which Israel did not plan to answer hastily; Eban proposed technical talks with Colonel Harkabi to end the airlift as soon as US needs allowed and suggested the Aqaba route, and said the most urgent issue was "the elimination of U.S. doubts about Israel's steadfastness."

Ben-Gurion's 5 August letter complained that "we have not been successful in receiving arms assistance from the United States" and that "we have never been granted a guarantee of our integrity", noting that the US assurance of help under the Eisenhower Doctrine had never been put in writing, and proposed closer ties among the countries of the periphery; Peres then set out Israel's arms needs.

The US airlift resumed on 6 August; on 10 August Dulles wrote that "we can consider the situation which arose out of the interruption of our flights a closed matter", Israel renewed the overflights, and Ben-Gurion wrote that he had gained "a free hand" in drafting the reply to Moscow.

JTA reported that Israel "apparently yielded to pressure from the United States" and that, according to Israeli sources, the ban had been prompted not by the Soviet note but "by British attempts to set Israel up as a bogey in the present crisis"; the same paper reported a new Soviet map placing Jerusalem and central Palestine in Jordan.

Schonmann calls the episode "the accidental crisis in American–Israeli relations": Dulles's letter and the Soviet note were dated the same day, and the Israeli stop order came before the US letter was delivered.

disputes.question: Why did Ben-Gurion stop the overflights on 2 August 1958?

positions.view: Fear of the Soviet note and cabinet pressure (Dulles's reading on 3 August; Lawson's report).

Not the Soviet note but domestic and British politics: the extra British troops were not crucial, and Britain was setting Israel up as 'a bogey' (Eban; Israeli sources to JTA; State's 5 August record).

entries.topic: West Germany and Israel, 1957–1962: the Strauss–Peres channel, the Waldorf meeting of March 1960 and 'Aktion Geschäftsfreund'

sources.label: Uri Bar-Joseph, "Historical Clues Indicate: Germany Secretly Funded Israel's Nuclear Program", Haaretz (13 March 2026), reposted by Portside (15 March 2026)
Michael Borchard, "Heute vor 65 Jahren: Ein Meilenstein der deutsch-israelischen Verständigung", Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung (14 March 2025)
Michael Brenner, "1960: Adenauer trifft Ben Gurion", Jüdische Allgemeine (28 January 2013)
Ralf Balke, "Von Adenauer bis Arrow 3", Jüdische Allgemeine (11 May 2025)
Rebecca M. Miller, "Did Germany Secretly Fund Israel's Nuclear Weapons?", The National Interest (undated)
FRUS 1958–1960, vol. XIII, doc. 119: Memorandum of a Conversation, Washington, 1 February 1960 (Ben-Gurion's request for an appointment with Eisenhower)

claims.text: Uri Bar-Joseph writes that Shimon Peres and West German Defence Minister Franz Josef Strauss met in Bonn on 3 July 1957, that Israel asked for two submarines, and that Strauss was ready to "build bridges" and interested in lessons from the Sinai war.

Bar-Joseph writes that the submarines were bought in Britain with German funding, for less than the cost of one French Vautour aircraft, and that Germany bought about $30 million of Israeli-made combat materiel.
Michael Brenner notes that Strauss and Peres, by 1960 Israel's deputy defence minister, had been in contact for years and spoke at the time of the Ben-Gurion–Adenauer meeting.

On 1 February 1960 Ambassador Harman asked Secretary Herter for a private meeting between Ben-Gurion and Eisenhower, suggesting an honorary degree from Brandeis University as the occasion so that Ben-Gurion could come "quietly"; Herter said an official invitation was out of the question, and a handwritten note records the President's approval of an appointment at 11 a.m. on 10 March 1960.

Ben-Gurion (73) and Chancellor Konrad Adenauer (84) met on 14 March 1960 in the presidential suite on the 35th floor of the Waldorf-Astoria in New York; no official transcript exists. Ben-Gurion said afterwards, "Das Deutschland von heute ist nicht das Deutschland von gestern" ("The Germany of today is not the Germany of yesterday"), against bitter opposition from many Israelis.

The Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung's historian writes that Ben-Gurion proposed economic aid of $500 million as a loan for Israel's further development and brought a wish list including guided missiles and submarines; Adenauer agreed to help without naming a sum.

According to Bar-Joseph, Ben-Gurion asked for $40–50 million a year for ten years; the loan agreed, code-named "Aktion Geschäftsfreund" ("Operation Business Friend"), was about $50 million a year for ten years at 3.6% interest, routed through a government-owned development bank in Frankfurt and booked as transfers under agreements with unnamed developing countries; the first payment came in December 1961.

German documents cited by Bar-Joseph give the transfers as 82 million marks in 1961, 97.6 million in 1962, 150 million in 1963, 149.8 million in 1964 and 150 million in 1965, 629.4 million marks in all to 1965; the Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung gives almost 630 million DM up to 1966, excluding weapons.
German documents put military-related aid and arms financing from 1962 to early 1965 ("Frank/Kol") at 340 million marks; the historian Roni Stauber (2022) puts it at 500 million marks (Bar-Joseph).

Bar-Joseph argues that West Germany was the "major funder" of Dimona through the Negev loan, but concedes that Israeli documentation on its use is missing and it is "impossible to assert unequivocally" that Bonn underwrote the reactor; The National Interest reports that Die Welt judged the funding "with near certainty", citing Strauss's claim that Ben-Gurion and Adenauer discussed the nuclear program in Paris in 1961, and that Peres had denied German funding.

On who paid for Dimona, Bar-Joseph reports Peres saying that about half the cost of the reactor and complex, about $40 million, came from donations by wealthy Jews; The National Interest reports Peres saying $40 million of Israeli government funds went to Dimona and that this was only half the cost.

Bar-Joseph writes that during the Eichmann trial Strauss stressed to Israeli officials that naming senior Bonn officials, especially Hans Globke, would jeopardize the arrangement, and quotes Peres as saying Ben-Gurion linked the Eichmann trial to the Dimona reactor.

Hans Globke, one of several figures around Adenauer with a Nazi-era past, had written commentaries on the Nuremberg Laws, and the minister Theodor Oberländer resigned a few months after the March 1960 meeting when his past became public (Brenner).

Bonn put off Israel's requests for diplomatic relations until 1965 for fear that Arab states would recognize East Germany; the secret arms deliveries became public in 1964 and military aid was temporarily halted, and relations were established on 12 May 1965.

disputes.question: Did the West German 'Negev' loan pay for Dimona?

positions.view: Probably, on indirect evidence (Bar-Joseph; Die Welt as reported by The National Interest).
Unproven: no Israeli record of its use, no transcript of the Waldorf meeting, Germany silent, Peres's denial; the Adenauer foundation describes it as development aid.

disputes.question: How much military aid did Germany give in 1962–65?

positions.view: 340 million marks (German documents).
500 million marks (Roni Stauber, 2022).
